title: Less Data, Faster Training: repeating smaller datasets speeds up learning via sampling biases
claim: Training repeatedly on a smaller dataset reaches low loss or high accuracy in fewer steps than training on a larger one, across many tasks.
layout: 4 panels in a row, each a curve plot with task name below
description: A single row of four line plots. Each plot has training steps on the x-axis and accuracy or test loss on the y-axis, with a task name under it: (a) sparse parity, (b) single-index model, (c) ICL linear regression, (d) modular addition. Every panel shows two curves with shaded variance bands. A blue curve is the large (online) dataset and an orange/yellow curve is the small dataset with an n-phase schedule, labeled 2-, 4- or 6-phase. In every panel the orange curve leaves the initial plateau sooner and converges much faster. In (a) and (d) the blue curve barely improves, while in (b) and (c) it lags well behind. The legend sits inside each plot. The orange curve is the first thing the eye follows.
caption: Small-vs-large gap exists in various tasks. Across various feature learning and algorithmic tasks (Section 3), training on a smaller dataset (yellow curves) leads to faster convergence than training on a larger dataset (blue curves). Results are based on 2-layer Transformers optimized with minibatched AdamW. An “n-phase” schedule denotes that the training set size is progressively increased over n phases (Section 3).
abstract: This work investigates the ``small-vs-large gap'', where repeating on fewer samples can lead to compute saving during training compared to using a larger dataset. This is observed across algorithmic tasks, architectures and optimizers and cannot be explained using prior theory. We argue that the speedup comes from appropriate layer-wise growth enabled by sampling biases, which is more pronounced when the dataset size is smaller. We provide both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence from various interventions. Our results suggest that using a smaller dataset with more repetitions is not just a fallback strategy under data scarcity, but can be proactively leveraged as a favorable inductive biases for optimization, particularly in reasoning tasks.
